old: A scepter-bearing king, whom Zeus has glorified, never shares in the common honor.
new: A king who holds the scepter, to whom Zeus has given glory, has never had an ordinary share of honor.
why: Greek 1.278-9 οὔ ποθ' ὁμοίης ἔμμορε τιμῆς σκηπτοῦχος βασιλεύς: his honor is above the common share. Butler: no sceptred king 'has like honour'. As printed it says he lacks honor.

old: And I was of their company, and they listened to my advice.
new: And I was of their company: I came from Pylos, from a far-off land, because they summoned me, and I fought on my own account. No one alive on earth today could fight those men. And they listened to my advice and heeded my word.
why: Greek 1.269-73 (ἐκ Πύλου ἐλθὼν τηλόθεν ... κείνοισι δ' ἂν οὔ τις τῶν οἳ νῦν βροτοί εἰσιν ... μαχέοιτο); Butler keeps it. Theseus (1.265) left out, as most editors bracket it.

old: Remind him: you once saved him, alone among the gods, when the others wanted to bind him. Go now, clasp his knees,
new: Often in my father's house I heard you boast that you alone among the gods saved the son of Cronus from shameful ruin, when the other Olympians wanted to put him in chains — Hera, and Poseidon, and Pallas Athena. You came, goddess, and freed him from the chains: you quickly called the hundred-handed one to high Olympus, the one the gods call Briareus and men call Aegaeon, stronger even than his father. He sat down beside the son of Cronus, glorying in his strength, and the blessed gods were afraid of him and did not bind Zeus. Remind him of that now. Sit beside him, clasp his knees,
why: Greek 1.396-407 restored: the would-be binders and the hundred-handed Briareus/Aegaeon (Butler seg-0036) were cut. Achilles' retelling (1.365-92), still summarized, goes to the editor (rejected.md).

old: why Apollo is so enraged. Maybe a vow, or a sacrifice, will buy us back from ruin.
new: why Apollo is so enraged: whether he blames us for some vow or sacrifice, and whether the smoke of lambs and full-grown goats might move him to keep ruin from us.
why: Greek 1.65-7 εἴτ' ἄρ' ὅ γ' εὐχωλῆς ἐπιμέμφεται εἴθ' ἑκατόμβης, αἴ κέν πως ἀρνῶν κνίσης αἰγῶν τε τελείων ...: a question about blame, with the savor of lambs and goats; Butler the same.

old: You gave her; take her back.
new: You gave her, and now you take her away.
why: Greek 1.299 ἐπεί μ' ἀφέλεσθέ γε δόντες: a bitter statement, not a command; Butler 'those that take were those also that gave'.

old: You shameless, scheming greed —
new: You, wrapped in shamelessness, always scheming for gain —
why: Greek 1.149 ἀναιδείην ἐπιειμένε, κερδαλεόφρον addresses the man, not an abstraction; 'you ... greed' does not land aloud.

old: and no one's hunger went unsatisfied at the shared feast — not for the gorgeous lyre Apollo held, nor for the Muses,
new: and no one's heart went without its share of the feast, or of the beautiful lyre Apollo held, or of the Muses,
why: Greek 1.602-4 οὐδέ τι θυμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης, οὐ μὲν φόρμιγγος ...: the heart lacked neither feast nor lyre; 'hunger ... for the lyre' garbles it; 'gorgeous' is fashionable.

old: while I'm alive and have my eyes
new: while I'm alive and see the light of day
why: Greek 1.88 ἐμεῦ ζῶντος καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ δερκομένοιο; Butler 'while I yet live to look upon the face of the earth'.

old: Don't try it, clever as you are, Achilles
new: Don't try it, Achilles, brave and godlike as you are
why: Greek 1.131 ἀγαθός περ ἐών, θεοείκελ' Ἀχιλλεῦ; Butler 'valiant though you be'. 'Clever' shifts the taunt.

old: with some small thing, worn out from war
new: with some small thing, small but my own, worn out from war
why: Greek 1.167 ὀλίγον τε φίλον τε: small but dear.

old: you've never spoken or carried out a single kind word
new: you've never once said a good word, or made one come true
why: Greek 1.108 οὐδέ τί πω μοι ἐσθλὸν εἶπας ἔπος οὐδ' ἐτέλεσσας; 'carried out a word' trips.

old: my untouchable hands
new: my invincible hands
why: Greek 1.567 ἀάπτους χεῖρας: hands none can withstand; 'untouchable' now reads as immunity.

old: who had guided the Greek ships to Troy by his prophecy
new: who had guided the Greek ships to Troy by the gift of prophecy Phoebus Apollo gave him
why: Greek 1.72 ἣν διὰ μαντοσύνην, τήν οἱ πόρε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων; Butler 'the prophetic gift with which Phoebus Apollo had inspired him'.

old: “Achilles, you tell me
new: “Achilles, dear to Zeus, you tell me
why: Greek 1.74 ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ, κέλεαί με, Διῒ φίλε.

old: Thersites kept on, a man with no measure to his tongue, his head full of words, reckless ones, set against the kings, in no good order, anything he thought would make the Greeks laugh.
new: Thersites kept on, a man with no measure to his tongue. His head was full of words, reckless and disorderly, for quarreling with kings — anything he thought would make the Greeks laugh.
why: Read-aloud: five tacked-on phrases lose the thread. Greek 2.213-15; Butler 'a man of many words, and those unseemly'.

old: that foul-spoken blowhard
new: that foul-mouthed slanderer
why: Policy (slang). Greek 2.275 λωβητῆρα ἐπεσβόλον: word-flinging abuser.

old: Now the other gods and the charioteers of the plain slept
new: Now the other gods and the men who fought from chariots slept
why: Greek 2.1 θεοί τε καὶ ἀνέρες ἱπποκορυσταί: 'men' dropped, 'of the plain' added.

old: you Trojans go on living here in the rich land of Troy, and the Greeks sail home to Argos and the green country of Achaea
new: you Trojans go on living here in the rich land of Troy, and the Greeks sail home to Argos, where the horses graze, and to Achaea of the lovely women
why: Greek 3.75 Ἄργος ἐς ἱππόβοτον καὶ Ἀχαιΐδα καλλιγύναικα; 'green country' is invented and the women are lost.

old: we Trojans live on here in the rich land of Troy, and the Greeks sail home to Argos and the green country of Achaea
new: we Trojans live on here in the rich land of Troy, and the Greeks sail home to Argos, where the horses graze, and to Achaea of the lovely women
why: Same formula, 3.258; see seg-0006.

old: Your heart is like an axe a shipwright drives through a beam, and the man's own strength gives the stroke its weight — that's how hard the edge of your scorn cuts.
new: Your heart is always unbending, like an axe a shipwright drives through a beam, the man's own strength giving the stroke its weight — that's how fearless the heart in your chest is.
why: Greek 3.60-63 αἰεί τοι κραδίη πέλεκυς ὥς ἐστιν ἀτειρής ... ὣς σοὶ ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἀτάρβητος νόος ἐστί: the simile is Hector's unyielding heart, not his scorn.

old: taking the shape of her sister-in-law — the wife of Antenor's son, for Helicaon had married Laodice, the loveliest of Priam's daughters.
new: taking the shape of her sister-in-law Laodice, the loveliest of Priam's daughters, wife of Antenor's son, lord Helicaon.
why: Greek 3.122-4 εἰδομένη γαλόῳ, Ἀντηνορίδαο δάμαρτι ... Λαοδίκην: name the shape Iris takes first.

old: three and four pieces
new: into three, four pieces
why: Greek 3.363 τριχθά τε καὶ τετραχθά; missing preposition trips.

old: with wings in their words
new: in winged words
why: Greek 3.155 ἔπεα πτερόεντ' ἀγόρευον; the edition's usual rendering is 'winged words' (e.g. II seg-0001).

old: the splendid car, and
new: the splendid chariot, and
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: Zeus, who holds the keys of war and peace for men,
new: Zeus, who deals out war to men,
why: Greek 4.84 Ζεύς, ὅς τ' ἀνθρώπων ταμίης πολέμοιο τέτυκται: steward of war; 'and peace' is added.

old: hacked at one another's shields, at the round bucklers and the light hide targets
new: hacked at one another's shields, the great round ones and the light, fluttering ones of hide
why: Policy (archaism). Greek 5.452-3 ἀσπίδας εὐκύκλους λαισήϊά τε πτερόεντα; 'targets' now means archery targets.

old: who owned much corn land
new: who owned much grain land
why: Policy (archaism). Greek 5.613 πολυλήϊος; 'corn' reads as maize to an American reader.

old: who did not shrink from his sins
new: who thought nothing of doing wrong
why: Policy (biblical idiom). Greek 5.403 ὃς οὐκ ὄθετ' αἴσυλα ῥέζων.

old: through the rings of his shirt
new: through his plaited tunic
why: Greek 5.113 διὰ στρεπτοῖο χιτῶνος; 'rings' suggests medieval mail.

old: from the car. Idaeus
new: from the chariot. Idaeus
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: toppled from the car; and Idomeneus'
new: toppled from the chariot; and Idomeneus'
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: from the car and pulled
new: from the chariot and pulled
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: from the car for all
new: from the chariot for all
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: fine new cars stand in
new: fine new chariots stand in
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: into the car — I'll
new: into the chariot — I'll
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: his own car again, gripped
new: his own chariot again, gripped
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

new: into the chariot, sick
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: the car headfirst,
new: the chariot headfirst,
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: side; the car was woven
new: side; the chariot was woven
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: mounted the car herself, beside
new: mounted the chariot herself, beside
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: up over the car, to fly
new: up over the chariot, to fly
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: Brother — brother of a hateful bitch of a woman, who brings on this horror.
new: Brother — brother-in-law to me, a hateful bitch of a woman, who brings on this horror.
why: Greek 6.344 δᾶερ ἐμεῖο κυνὸς κακομηχάνου ὀκρυοέσσης: Helen calls herself the bitch; as printed, Hector seems brother to some third woman.

old: "You strange woman — don't grieve too much
new: "My dearest — don't grieve too much
why: Policy (δαιμόνιε). Greek 6.486 δαιμονίη in Hector's gentlest moment, just after he strokes her; 'You strange woman' reads cold.

old: the long cuts of the chine to honor him
new: the long cuts of the back to honor him
why: Policy (archaism). Greek 7.321 νώτοισιν ... διηνεκέεσσι γέραιρεν.

old: you reckless, brazen thing
new: you shameless bitch
why: Greek 8.423 αἰνοτάτη, κύον ἀδεές; the edition keeps Helen's 'bitch' in VI and should keep it here.

old: the hound of hell
new: the hound of hateful Hades
why: Policy (biblical/Christian frame). Greek 8.368 κύνα στυγεροῦ Ἀΐδαο.

old: I won’t care a whit how angry you are
new: I won’t care in the least how angry you are
why: Policy (archaism). 'A whit'.

old: from the car. Grief
new: from the chariot. Grief
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: under the car, and
new: under the chariot, and
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: forward from the car.
new: forward from the chariot.
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: headlong from the car, and the
new: headlong from the chariot, and the
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: them out, and smash the car to pieces. Ten full years
new: them out, and smash the chariot to pieces. Ten full years
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: you out, and smash the car to pieces. Ten full years
new: you out, and smash the chariot to pieces. Ten full years
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: set the car on its
new: set the chariot on its
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: I hate that man like the gates of death who says one thing and hides another in his heart.
new: I hate like the gates of death the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another.
why: Greek 9.312-13 ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοι κεῖνος ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσιν ὅς χ' ἕτερον μὲν κεύθῃ ἐνὶ φρεσίν, ἄλλο δὲ εἴπῃ; the relative clause landed on 'death'.

old: “All hail — and welcome. You must come on some pressing need.
new: “Welcome, both of you. You come as friends — there must be some great need.
why: Greek 9.197 χαίρετον· ἦ φίλοι ἄνδρες ἱκάνετον· ἦ τι μάλα χρεώ; 'All hail' is stage archaism and 'as friends' was dropped.

old: since the day — yes, royal as you are — that you went
new: since the day, my king, that you went
why: Greek 9.106 διογενές is a respectful vocative; the parenthesis reads as sarcasm.

old: the chine of a hog rich with fat
new: the backbone of a hog, rich with fat
why: Policy (archaism). Greek 9.208 συὸς σιάλοιο ῥάχιν τεθαλυῖαν ἀλοιφῇ.

old: the son of Aeacus would
new: the grandson of Aeacus would
why: Policy (patronymics): Greek Αἰακίδης, descendant of Aeacus; Achilles is Peleus's son. The edition already says 'grandson of Aeacus' in II and XVII.

old: never filled with cunning or with toil
new: who can never get enough of tricks and toil
why: Greek 11.430 δόλων ἆτ' ἠδὲ πόνοιο: insatiable of tricks; 'never filled with cunning' is heard as 'never cunning'.

old: Here comes great Hector, rolling down on us — we're for it.
new: Here comes great Hector — disaster rolling down on us.
why: Greek 11.347 νῶϊν δὴ τόδε πῆμα κυλίνδεται; 'we're for it' is British slang.

old: two men bit the dust on my spear
new: two men bit the earth on my spear
why: Policy (slang): Homer's own image is ὀδὰξ ἕλον οὖδας, bit the ground; II seg-0027 already has 'bitten the earth'. (11.749)

old: Achilles, son of Aeacus.
new: Achilles, grandson of Aeacus.
why: Policy (patronymics): Greek Αἰακίδης, descendant of Aeacus; Achilles is Peleus's son. The edition already says 'grandson of Aeacus' in II and XVII.

old: old Ilus, son of Dardanus, in
new: old Ilus, of the line of Dardanus, in
why: Policy (patronymics): Greek Δαρδανίδης, of Dardanus's line; Priam is Laomedon's son, Ilus is Tros's. Matches III seg-0027 'Priam of the line of Dardanus'.

old: for Ilus, son of Dardanus, a
new: for Ilus, of the line of Dardanus, a
why: Policy (patronymics): Greek Δαρδανίδης, of Dardanus's line; Priam is Laomedon's son, Ilus is Tros's. Matches III seg-0027 'Priam of the line of Dardanus'.

old: him from the car. He stripped
new: him from the chariot. He stripped
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: from the car and begged:
new: from the chariot and begged:
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: around the car splashed with
new: around the chariot splashed with
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: fought on without let
new: fought on without pause
why: Policy (archaism). 'Without let'.

old: whom the great tawny horses of the Selleis breed had carried from Arisbe
new: whom his great sorrel horses had carried from Arisbe, from the river Selleis
why: Greek 12.96-7 οὓς Ἀρίσβηθεν φέρον ἵπποι αἴθωνες μεγάλοι, ποταμοῦ ἄπο Σελλήεντος; there is no Selleis breed (II seg-0069 has it right).

old: the proud Hippemolgi who milk their mares, and the Abians, the justest men alive, who live on milk and shed no blood.
new: the proud Hippemolgi, who live on milk, and the Abians, the justest men alive.
why: Greek 13.5-6 Ἱππημολγῶν γλακτοφάγων Ἀβίων τε δικαιοτάτων ἀνθρώπων: 'milk their mares' glosses the name, 'shed no blood' is invented, and the milk belongs to the Hippemolgi (Butler).

old: Meriones, his sturdy aide
new: Meriones, his sturdy squire
why: Greek θεράπων; the edition's word elsewhere is squire (XVII seg-0019, XXIII seg-0050); 'aide' sounds like a staffer.

old: him and his aide
new: him and his squire
why: As seg-0017.

old: bound the hand up in a twist of well-spun wool, a sling the aide of that shepherd of the people carried.
new: bound the hand up in a sling of well-spun wool that his squire carried for him, the shepherd of the people.
why: Greek 13.599-600 σφενδόνῃ, ἣν ἄρα οἱ θεράπων φέρε ποιμένι λαῶν; the inverted clause stacked two titles and tripped.

old: Strange man, come stand and face me yourself
new: Madman, come stand and face me yourself
why: Policy (δαιμόνιε). Greek 13.448, a battle taunt.

old: "You strange man, come closer.
new: "You madman, come closer.
why: Policy (δαιμόνιε). Greek 13.810, a battle taunt.

old: but you, I am furious with.
new: but with you I am furious.
why: Greek 13.119 ὑμῖν δὲ νεμεσσῶμαι περὶ κῆρι; the inverted ending lost its stress.

old: Paris, you misery, fine to look at, woman-mad, smooth talker
new: Cursed Paris, fine to look at, woman-mad seducer
why: Greek 13.769 Δύσπαρι ... γυναιμανές, ἠπεροπευτά (the same line as III, rendered there 'you cursed, pretty Paris'); 'you misery' is not English.

old: Priam, son of Dardanus,
new: Priam, of the line of Dardanus,
why: Policy (patronymics): Greek Δαρδανίδης, of Dardanus's line; Priam is Laomedon's son, Ilus is Tros's. Matches III seg-0027 'Priam of the line of Dardanus'.

old: they took me in and raised me in their own house
new: they took me from Rhea and raised me in their own house
why: Greek 14.202-3 δεξάμενοι Ῥείας; Butler 'having taken me over from Rhaea'.

old: the Trojans driving them before it.
new: the Trojans driving them on from behind.
why: Greek 14.14-15 κλονέοντας ὄπισθε Τρῶας; 'before it' made the wall the subject.

old: without let or pause
new: without rest or pause
why: Policy (archaism). 'Without let'.

old: the painted car. They
new: the painted chariot. They
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: The Greeks held firm against the Trojans' attack, and though the Trojans were the fewer, they could not drive the Greeks back from the ships;
new: The Greeks held firm against the Trojans' attack, but though the Trojans were the fewer, the Greeks could not drive them back from the ships;
why: Subject reversed. Greek 15.405-7 Ἀχαιοὶ δὲ Τρῶας ἐπερχομένους μένον ἔμπεδον, οὐδ' ἐδύναντο παυροτέρους περ ἐόντας ἀπώσασθαι παρὰ νηῶν: the Greeks could not push back the fewer Trojans.

old: thrown into godlike panic
new: thrown into a wild, unearthly panic
why: Greek 15.637 θεσπεσίως ἐφόβηθεν: the adverb means wondrously, terribly; Butler 'utterly panic-stricken'.

old: From that poor father came a far better son
new: From that far meaner father came a far better son
why: Greek 15.641 ἐκ πατρὸς πολὺ χείρονος υἱὸς ἀμείνων; 'poor' reads as pitiable.

old: the empty car. Polydamas
new: the empty chariot. Polydamas
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: you are only the third to take my armor.
new: you come only third in the killing of me.
why: Greek 16.850 σὺ δέ με τρίτος ἐξεναρίζεις: third to slay me (Butler 'third only in the killing of me'). Apollo stripped the armor, Euphorbus took none, so the printed line contradicts itself.

old: God keep me from a rage like the one you nurse
new: May no rage like the one you nurse ever take hold of me
why: Policy (biblical idiom). Greek 16.30 μὴ ἐμέ γ' οὗτός γε λάβοι χόλος ὃν σὺ φυλάσσεις.

old: who was no worst among the Myrmidons
new: who was far from the worst of the Myrmidons
why: Ungrammatical. Greek 16.570 οὔ τι κάκιστος.

old: as if I were some nobody with no honor at all
new: as if I were some drifter with no honor at all
why: Greek 16.59 ὡς εἴ τιν' ἀτίμητον μετανάστην: a dishonored vagrant (Butler 'a vagrant').

old: the swift-footed son of Aeacus, starry
new: the swift-footed grandson of Aeacus, starry
why: Policy (patronymics): Greek Αἰακίδης, descendant of Aeacus; Achilles is Peleus's son. The edition already says 'grandson of Aeacus' in II and XVII.

why: Policy (patronymics): Greek Αἰακίδης, descendant of Aeacus; Achilles is Peleus's son. The edition already says 'grandson of Aeacus' in II and XVII.

why: Policy (patronymics): Greek Αἰακίδης, descendant of Aeacus; Achilles is Peleus's son. The edition already says 'grandson of Aeacus' in II and XVII.

new: tumbled from the chariot, and the
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

new: masters' chariots behind.
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

new: rail of the chariot — the way

why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: That great name of yours is wasted; you're a runner.
new: That great name of yours is wasted on a man who runs away.
why: Greek 17.143 φύξηλιν ἐόντα: a runaway; 'runner' reads as an athlete.

old: strips the win from him
new: strips the victory from him
why: Policy (sports-page 'win'). Greek 17.177 ἀφείλετο νίκην.

why: Policy (patronymics): Greek Αἰακίδης, descendant of Aeacus; Achilles is Peleus's son. The edition already says 'grandson of Aeacus' in II and XVII.

old: the sacred car, both
new: the sacred chariot, both
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

new: from the chariot and fight.”
why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

old: They moved to hold him up as he came near Thetis, sat her on a fine chair, took her hand, and said:
new: They moved busily to hold their master up, and he limped near to where Thetis was, sat down on a shining chair, took her hand, and said:
why: Speaker wrong. Greek 18.421-4 αἳ μὲν ὕπαιθα ἄνακτος ἐποίπνυον· αὐτὰρ ὁ ἔρρων πλησίον ... ἐπὶ θρόνου ἷζε φαεινοῦ, ἔν τ' ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρί: Hephaestus himself sits, takes her hand and speaks (Butler likewise). Charis had already seated Thetis (seg-0028); the speech's 'Tell me ... my heart says do it' is his.

old: the huge, sooty creature
new: the huge, hulking god
why: Greek 18.410 πέλωρ αἴητον: a huge, monstrous figure; 'sooty' is added (Butler 'the mighty monster').

old: the son of Aeacus.
new: the grandson of Aeacus.
why: Policy (patronymics): Greek Αἰακίδης, descendant of Aeacus; Achilles is Peleus's son. The edition already says 'grandson of Aeacus' in II and XVII.

old: had run him through with a spear in the battle
new: had wounded him with a spear in the battle
why: Greek 19.53 οὔτασε: wounded. In XI (11.252-3) the spear went through his forearm, not his body; Butler 'had wounded him'.

old: I will not take the name of the gods in vain
new: I will not swear falsely before the gods
why: Policy (biblical idiom). Greek 19.188 οὐδ' ἐπιορκήσω πρὸς δαίμονος.

new: however much his heart is set on fighting, his limbs grow heavy before he knows it

old: Sigh broke from him after sigh
new: Sigh after sigh broke from him
why: Inverted order trips aloud.

old: would not have bitten the dust
new: would not have bitten the earth
why: Policy (slang): Homer's own image is ὀδὰξ ἕλον οὖδας, bit the ground; II seg-0027 already has 'bitten the earth'. (19.61)

why: Policy (archaism): 'car' for chariot (δίφρος, ἅρμα, ὄχεα); today it means an automobile.

new: My spear too has been found sharp before now.
why: Greek 20.437 ἐπεὶ ἦ καὶ ἐμὸν βέλος ὀξὺ πάροιθεν; 'this' had no antecedent.

old: fool that he was, his mind missing it: that the glorious gifts
new: fool that he was, not to see in his heart that the glorious gifts
why: Greek 20.264-5 νήπιος, οὐδ' ἐνόησε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν ὡς ...; the colon splice tangled the aside.

new: saw huge Achilles below
